newsitem.title: MEXICO: Demand rises for Mexico Cetes at attractive rates.
newsitem.headline: Demand rises for Mexico Cetes at attractive rates.

text.p: Demand surged for Mexican Treasury bills (Cetes) in Tuesday's auction, helping moderate what had been expected to be a sharp rate rise even though benchmark 28-day paper edged up slightly.
"It was a very positive auction that was in a way not surprising," said Gene Frieda of I.D.E.A. in New York. "You haven't seen these kinds of real yields in a long time."
Demand was most robust at 91 and 182 days, with bid-to-cover ratios of 6.97 and 6.88, respectively, up from 4.55 and 6.7 last week when rates rose sharply.

Earlier in the day, analysts in a Reuters survey had expected both maturities to rise more than 30 basis points, but 91-day paper actually fell one basis point to 22.97 percent and the six-month issue was unchanged at 22.99 percent.
The benchmark 28-day rate rose 28 basis points to 22.61 percent, and the one-year rate was also up at 24.29 percent.
Analysts and traders had expected a sharp rate rise because of volatility in the U.S. Treasury market and a large drain of liquidity at high rates by Banco de Mexico on Monday.
But favourable U.S. inflation data on Tuesday helped soothe fears of an imminent hike in U.S. rates and calmed the U.S. Treasury market. The upbeat mood swept into Mexico.
Frieda, who is bullish on the Mexican Cetes market, said part of its strong performance was due to the peso holding up well during the chaotic U.S. rate environment.
"Given the resilience of the peso after what U.S. rates had done, it's not surprising (some) rates came in lower and you have this kind of demand."
He said he would not be surprised if rates fell next week, though given the cloudiness of the U.S. market, he was not prepared to risk a longer-term forecast.

Scott Grimberg, Latin American economist at MMS International, said rates may remain steady next week, though he also worried about the possible fallout from more weakness in the U.S. Treasury market.
In Tuesday's auction, he said the fact that 28-day rates rose continued to reflect the U.S. rate uncertainty and "the medium-term vulnerability of the peso".
But for the time being, the peso's firmness was providing decent peso liquidity, which in turn helped underpin demand for Cetes, he said.
